cells.tense: Right now you're standing with the pen in your hand, in the middle of something you started without seeing all of it.
cells.ask: Take the one step that's already visible today, and write down one sentence afterward about what it showed you — the ground handing over a fact instead of a promise.
cells.core:
You can begin something without needing its whole shape first. Enough light shows, you go by that, and you correct as you walk. That's not sloppy planning — it's how an unclear thing actually gets finished. What you're carrying now came together that way, one visible step at a time, and it holds.

What this balance can feed next is another beginning on the same terms: not because you feel ready, but because the next stretch of ground is in front of you. The move is one step, then looking at what it gave you. There's a small satisfaction in that, and it asks nothing else of you.

cells.tense: You're leaning into a future you're already trying to finish before it arrives.
cells.ask: Before you act on one half-formed plan today, write down only what you can see in front of you — no filling in what isn't there. Notice what the plain looking clears.
cells.core:
You're trying to see the whole road before you take the first step. The next move gets planned, rethought, and pre-finished in your head, and you carry the weight of all of it at once. The not-knowing stops being something you move through and becomes something you fight, and the fight is what's tiring you.

Going well, this looks like a person in a kitchen mid-recipe: tasting as they go, adjusting the heat, not needing the finished plate in mind to keep cooking. Enough light for the next step, trusted. That's how anyone moves in fog — by noticing what's already visible and going. What helps is smaller than you'd expect: look at what's here, not at what you're bracing for. What that leaves you is a lighter load and a truer next move.

cells.tense: You're standing at a threshold you've already walked past, still waiting for it to open.
cells.ask: Let one thing reach you before you understand it — a person, a piece of work, a song — and stay with it for a minute without deciding what it means. Notice what moves.
cells.core:
When this is working, you're the one who leans into a half-finished conversation and doesn't rush it shut, who follows a melody without needing to know where it lands. You let things come to you at their own speed, and that reception is doing real work.

Lately the stepping has stopped. Things still start, but you're not inside them while they run — you watch from a little distance, and the distance feels safer than the next move. Nothing arrives at full weight. There's still a road; your foot just isn't on it. What's left open is the part before understanding: being moved by something first, then answering from there. Letting one thing land before you've sorted it gives back the contact you've been holding off.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped stepping into the unclear.

cells.tense: You're already reading the fog and steering by it while the pen stays down.
cells.ask: Say one sentence out loud about a choice you made this week without knowing how it would go — call it yours, plainly, to one person or into the quiet of the room you're in.
cells.core:
At its most ordinary, this is driving a familiar road at night: you don't see past your headlights, and you keep driving anyway, and you get there. You do that. You trust the small light and the small light carries you.

What's unowned is that it's you doing it. You feel your way, adjust, and it works — and the story you tell is that it happened to you, or that it was luck or instinct. You steer under everything. You just don't call it that. Naming one choice as yours costs a sentence and hands back the part of you that's been doing this all along, now standing where you can see it.
cells.sheetLine: You've been steering through the fog. You haven't said so.
